newsitem.title: DOMINICAN REPUBLIC: Peru, Dominican Republic discuss rebel asylum.
newsitem.headline: Peru, Dominican Republic discuss rebel asylum.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori discussed the possibility of asylum in the Dominincan Republic for Marxist rebels in a meeting with President Leonel Fernandez on Sunday, a government source said.

Fujimori flew in to Santo Domingo for a lightning one-day trip to discuss the crisis in Lima where 20-odd Marxist guerrillas have been holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's Lima residence for 75 days.

Asked whether Fujimori and Fernandez spoke of a possibile Dominican asylum for the rebels in a 3 1/2 hour meeting here, a source close to Fernandez said, "We are discussing that possibility but there is nothing concrete yet."
Fujimori told reporters that the two governments would issue a joint communique within hours.

Dominican Interior Minister Norge Botello said before Fujimori arrived that the Dominican Republic would be prepared to offer the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas asylum if Peru requested it.
But Fujimori said in an interview broadcast on Sunday in Peru that the Dominican Republic would not be a likely destination for the rebels.
"I don't think the Dominican Republic will be acceptable to them (rebels) as a destination," Fujimori said in the interview aired on local television.
"It's possible that in a third country at some moment it may be necessary and so we're talking about that in an informal way," he added.

News reports have touted Cuba, Nicaragua or Eastern Europe as possible refuges in a deal to end Latin America's longest hostage siege. Fujimori said he has not spoken to Cuba's President Fidel Castro about asylum for the guerrillas.
Fujimori arrived on Sunday afternoon in Santo Domingo on a plane packed with reporters as well as his teenage son Kenji and a group of schoolmates.

It was his second visit to the Caribbean nation in less than a month, after he met Fernandez during a surprise four-hour stopover at Santo Domingo airport on Feb. 5 on his way back from a trip to Canada.

The heavily-armed squad of Cuban-inspired guerrillas stormed a cocktail party at the Japanese ambassador's residence on Dec. 17. They swiftly freed hundreds of hostages but still hold two of Fujimori's relatives, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia, and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
